title: How Edison Lost The War Of The Currents To Westinghouse And Tesla
sources: Smithsonian / Library of Congress: Pearl Street Station opened 4 Sep 1882 (~400 lamps); DC range about a mile

PBS American Experience 'Tesla' / Smithsonian Magazine: Tesla arrived 1884, left Edison after ~6 months ($50,000 claim is Tesla's account); AC patents 1888; Westinghouse licence (~$60,000 + $2.50/hp royalty, reported); later buyout ~$216,000 (W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla: Inventor of the Electrical Age)
Edison letter to Edward Johnson, Nov 1886 ('Just as certain as death...'), Thomas A. Edison Papers, Rutgers

Harold P. Brown: Evening Post letter June 1888, Columbia demonstrations July 1888, letters published by The Sun 25 Aug 1889; Kemmler executed 6 Aug 1890 Auburn (two shocks); Westinghouse 'axe' remark as reported (Jill Jonnes, Empires of Light; Tom McNichol, AC/DC)
John Feeks death on overhead wires, lower Manhattan, 11 Oct 1889 (New York Times archive)

General Electric formed 1892 (Edison General Electric + Thomson-Houston; Coffin president); 1893 Chicago Exposition lit by Westinghouse AC; Niagara (Adams plant) power to Buffalo Nov 1896 (IEEE Milestone)
Westinghouse lost control of his company after the Panic of 1907; Tesla died Jan 1943, Hotel New Yorker; Con Edison ended last DC service 14 Nov 2007 (NYT)
Topsy (Luna Park, 4 Jan 1903): film by Edison Manufacturing Co.; no evidence Edison was involved (Smithsonian)
Footage/photos: Library of Congress (Westinghouse Works 1904 films, PD), Wikimedia Commons public-domain pre-1928 images, Edison films (PD)
Hedged in script: $50,000 promise (Tesla's account), licence price 'reported', axe remark 'reported', royalty tear-up 'the story goes', Niagara distance '20+ miles', fair lamps 'tens of thousands'

beats.text: New York. October 1889. Lunchtime on a busy street in lower Manhattan.
High above the crowd, a lineman named John Feeks is working in a tangle of wires.

v.q: tangle of overhead wires New York 1888

beats.text: He touches the wrong one. And the people below look up and watch him die.
For one inventor's camp, this is proof of what they have been saying for months. Alternating current kills.
That inventor is the most famous man in America. Thomas Edison.
And he is losing a business war he started, to a rival who never wanted a war at all.
This is how the greatest inventor of his age fought dirty, lost anyway, and was pushed out of his own company.
Go back to September 1882. Edison opens the Pearl Street power station in Manhattan.
On the first day it lights about four hundred lamps. Electric light, sold like gas or water.
Edison's system uses direct current, or DC. The power flows one way, at low voltage. It is safe and it works.
But DC has one big weakness. It cannot travel far. Edison needs a power station about every mile.
For a city, that is fine. For a whole country, it means thousands of stations, and a fortune in thick copper wire.
Edison does not see a problem. He owns the patents, the factories and the name.
In 1884, a tall young engineer from what is now Croatia arrives in New York to work for him.
His name is Nikola Tesla. He has an idea in his head for a motor that runs on alternating current.
Alternating current, or AC, flips direction many times a second. With a transformer, it can be pushed to high voltage and sent for miles.
Edison is not interested. Tesla later said he was promised fifty thousand dollars to improve Edison's machines, and was told it was a joke.
That is Tesla's side of the story. What we know for sure is that he quit after about six months.
For a while, he digs ditches to survive. Then, in 1888, his AC motor patents are granted.
One man reads them and sees the future. George Westinghouse, a Pittsburgh millionaire who made his money on train air brakes.
Westinghouse has already bought rights to a European transformer design, and his engineer William Stanley has lit up a street with AC in Great Barrington, Massachusetts.
Now he buys Tesla's patents. The deal is reported at about sixty thousand dollars, plus a royalty for every horsepower sold.
AC is cheaper. It needs fewer stations and thinner wire. Towns start choosing Westinghouse.
Edison sees his business at risk. And he decides the way to win is to make people afraid.
In a private letter, he had already written that just as certain as death, Westinghouse would kill a customer within six months.

v.text: Just as certain as death Westinghouse will kill a customer within six months.

beats.text: In June 1888, a little-known electrician named Harold Brown writes to a New York paper. He says AC is deadly and should be limited by law.
That summer, Brown gives public shows at Columbia College, using high-voltage AC on animals to prove his point.
It is ugly, and it works. The newspapers love it.
Brown says he is an independent expert. He is not. He has been given help and space at Edison's laboratory in West Orange, New Jersey.
Then the campaign finds a bigger stage. New York State is looking for a new way to carry out executions.
Edison backs electricity, and he points officials to alternating current. He even testifies that AC would kill a man instantly.
Behind the scenes, Brown gets hold of Westinghouse generators for the electric chair, even though Westinghouse refuses to sell them for that.
The point is clear. If the chair runs on Westinghouse power, every family will fear a Westinghouse wire in their home.
In August 1889, the New York Sun prints Brown's stolen letters. They show he has been working with Edison's side all along.
But the plan keeps moving. In August 1890, at Auburn Prison, William Kemmler becomes the first person executed with electricity.
The first shock does not kill him. Witnesses are horrified. It takes a second, longer shock.
Westinghouse is reported to have said they would have done better using an axe.

v.text: They would have done better using an axe.

beats.text: Edison's side even pushed the word 'Westinghoused' to mean electrocuted. It never caught on.
The fear campaign makes headlines. But it does not change the maths. AC keeps winning contracts.
And Edison has a bigger problem. His company needs money, and the money belongs to bankers like J. P. Morgan.
In 1892, Edison General Electric is merged with its rival Thomson-Houston. The new company is called General Electric.
Edison's name is gone from the company. The boss is Thomson-Houston's Charles Coffin. And the new company sells AC too.
The man who started the war has been taken out of it by his own investors.
The war is settled in public. Chicago, 1893. The World's Columbian Exposition.
Westinghouse bids to light the whole fair, far below General Electric's price, and wins.
On opening day, the President presses a button, and the fairground comes alive.
At night, tens of thousands of lamps glow over the White City. All of it running on AC.

v.q: Court of Honor Columbian Exposition night

beats.text: Millions of visitors see it with their own eyes. AC is not a killer. It is the future.
Then comes the biggest prize of all. Niagara Falls.
The power company picks Westinghouse and Tesla's system to turn the falls into electricity.
In November 1896, power from Niagara reaches Buffalo, more than twenty miles away. Edison's DC could never do that.
The war of the currents is over. AC has won.
But here is the twist. Not one of the three men got the ending he deserved.
Westinghouse's company was hit by money trouble in the early 1890s. The story goes that Tesla tore up his royalty contract to save it.
Records show Westinghouse later bought the patents outright, for about two hundred and sixteen thousand dollars. Tesla lost the royalties that could have made him rich.
Tesla died alone in a New York hotel room in January 1943, in debt.
Westinghouse lost control of his own company after another crash, the Panic of 1907.
And Edison? He moved on to film, sound and other inventions. He stayed rich and famous. But he never ran the power business again.
There is also a famous myth. People say Edison electrocuted Topsy the elephant in 1903 to attack AC.
The war was over a decade before that. A film company with Edison's name recorded it, but historians find no sign he was involved.
And here is the strangest part. Edison's direct current never fully died.
In New York, Con Edison kept DC customers in Manhattan for more than a century. The last one was cut off in November 2007.
And today, your phone, your laptop and every solar panel and battery run on DC. Giant DC lines now carry power across countries.
AC won the grid. DC won the gadgets.
Edison fought dirty to protect one business, and lost. The real winner was the company built by bankers, General Electric.
